subject: physics

items.q: Which statement expresses the principle of the conservation of energy?
items.correct: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so the total energy of an isolated system stays constant.
items.misconception: Energy is conserved until it is used up in doing work, after which it no longer exists.
items.why: Everyday language talks of 'using energy', 'running out of energy' and energy being 'lost', and people pay for energy that seems to be consumed. What is actually 'used up' is the usefulness of the energy, not the energy itself. The total energy of an isolated system is constant. When a ball stops bouncing or a motor warms up, energy has been transferred to the internal energy of the objects and the air, and to sound. It is dissipated, not destroyed; every joule can still be accounted for.
items.specStatementText: the principle of the conservation of energy
items.random_wrong: Each object in a system keeps the same amount of energy throughout any process.

items.q: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 2.0 m onto a hard floor and rebounds to a height of 1.5 m. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement correctly accounts for the energy?
items.correct: The total is unchanged; a quarter of the ball's mechanical energy became internal energy and sound.
items.misconception: Mechanical energy is conserved, so the missing quarter is still stored as elastic potential energy in the ball.
items.why: The principle of conservation of energy (total energy) and conservation of mechanical energy are both called 'energy conservation', and students do not separate the special case from the general principle. Total energy is always conserved; mechanical energy is conserved only without non-conservative forces doing work. With friction, ΔE_mech = W_nc < 0 and the 'missing' mechanical energy is found as internal energy.
items.specStatementText: the principle of the conservation of energy
items.random_wrong: Energy was not conserved in the bounce, because a quarter of the ball's energy was used up and destroyed.

items.q: A weightlifter holds a barbell stationary above her head for 4.0 s. How much work does she do on the barbell during these 4.0 s?
items.correct: None, because the barbell does not move, so no energy is transferred to it.
items.misconception: A large amount, because holding the heavy barbell up takes a great deal of effort.
items.why: In everyday language 'work' means effort or tiredness. Holding a heavy load is tiring because muscle fibres repeatedly contract, transferring chemical energy to internal energy inside the body, but none of that is transferred to the load. Work done on a body is W = Fs cos θ. If the displacement s is zero, the work done on the body is zero, however large the force and however long it acts. The body's energy is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: that work done by a force is equivalent to a transfer of energy
items.random_wrong: Her upward force multiplied by the 4.0 s for which she holds it up.

items.q: Work done and energy are both measured in joules. Which statement correctly defines one joule of work done?
items.correct: The work done when a force of 1 N moves its point of application 1 m in the direction of the force.
items.misconception: The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body for a time of 1 s, whether or not the body moves at all.
items.why:
Students meet F × s and F × Δt (impulse) in the same topic and both look like 'force times something'. Lawson and McDermott (1987) documented students confusing the work–energy and impulse–momentum theorems. Work is force times displacement along the line of the force. A large force acting for a long time on a stationary object does no work; a force acting for a short time over a large displacement can do a great deal of work.

Working: W = Fs cos θ = (1 N)(1 m)(cos 0°) = 1 N m = 1 J.
items.specStatementText: that work done by a force is equivalent to a transfer of energy
items.random_wrong: The work done when a force of 1 N acts on a body that moves 1 m in any direction relative to that force.
items.working: W = Fs cos θ = (1 N)(1 m)(cos 0°) = 1 N m = 1 J.

items.q: A student draws a Sankey diagram for an electric motor. The input arrow is 50 mm wide and represents 100 J of electrical energy. Only two output arrows are drawn: one 20 mm wide for work done lifting a load, and one 25 mm wide for thermal energy transferred to the surroundings. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
items.correct: An arrow 5 mm wide is missing; it represents 10 J, since the outputs must total 100 J.
items.misconception: An arrow is missing, but it only represents 5 J, as 1 mm of width stands for 1 J.
items.why:
Many textbook Sankey diagrams are drawn with an input of 100 J or 100 units on 1 mm per unit, so the width, the energy and the percentage are all the same number. Students learn the shortcut, not the reason it worked. Always find the scale first (for example, input energy ÷ input width) and convert widths to energies with it. To find a percentage or efficiency, divide by the actual input energy, not by 100.

Working: Scale = 100 J / 50 mm = 2 J mm⁻¹. Outputs drawn = 20 mm + 25 mm = 45 mm = 90 J. Missing = 50 mm − 45 mm = 5 mm = 5 mm × 2 J mm⁻¹ = 10 J.
items.specStatementText: that energy transfers can be represented on a Sankey diagram
items.random_wrong: No arrow is missing; the other 10 J was used up inside the motor and is gone.
items.working: Scale = 100 J / 50 mm = 2 J mm⁻¹. Outputs drawn = 20 mm + 25 mm = 45 mm = 90 J. Missing = 50 mm − 45 mm = 5 mm = 5 mm × 2 J mm⁻¹ = 10 J.

items.q: Which statement is true of every correctly drawn Sankey diagram?
items.correct: The widths of the output arrows add up to the width of the input arrow.
items.misconception: The longest arrow on the diagram represents the largest transfer of energy.
items.why: Most diagrams students meet that show quantities are bar charts, where length encodes the value, so they carry that reading over to Sankey arrows. Read a Sankey diagram by width. The arrows can be drawn with any length and can bend; the energy or power represented is proportional to the arrow's width, using the diagram's scale.
items.specStatementText: that energy transfers can be represented on a Sankey diagram
items.random_wrong: The output arrows are narrower in total than the input, as energy is used up.

items.q: A child pulls a sledge 25 m along level snow using a rope held at 30° above the horizontal. The tension in the rope is a constant 80 N. How much work does the tension do on the sledge?
items.why:
At GCSE work is taught as 'force × distance moved in the direction of the force', and the direction condition is dropped in memory, leaving 'force × distance'. Resolve the force along the line of displacement. W = Fs cos θ gives the full Fs only when the force is along the displacement (θ = 0), zero when it is perpendicular, and a negative value when it opposes the displacement.

Working: W = Fs cos θ = (80 N)(25 m)(cos 30°) = 2000 × 0.866 = 1732 J ≈ 1.7 × 10³ J.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ

items.q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.60 m at constant speed on a smooth, horizontal table. The tension in the string is 12 N. How much work does the tension do on the stone during one complete revolution?
items.correct: Zero, because the tension is perpendicular to the stone's displacement at every instant.
items.misconception: A positive amount, because the tension is the force that keeps the stone moving.
items.why: Everyday objects slow down unless pushed, because friction and air resistance act, so people form an 'impetus' view that motion itself requires a force. This is one of the most thoroughly documented misconceptions in mechanics (e.g. Halloun and Hestenes, 1985). At constant velocity the forces are balanced: the pull equals friction. With zero resultant force, the resultant force does no work and the kinetic energy stays constant. A resultant force is needed only to change the speed or direction.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ
items.random_wrong: About 45 J, which is the tension multiplied by the full circumference of the circular path.

items.q: A trolley moves 4.0 m in a straight line. One of the forces acting on it is a constant 20 N force directed at 120° to the trolley's displacement. How much work does this force do on the trolley?
items.why:
'Scalar' is taken to mean 'positive', and in everyday use work is always something done, never undone, so a negative amount of work seems meaningless. Work is a signed scalar. Friction on a sliding block, or the tension in a rope lowering a load, does negative work: energy is transferred out of the body's kinetic or potential energy. The sign carries the direction of the energy transfer.

Working: W = Fs cos θ = (20 N)(4.0 m)(cos 120°) = 80 × (−0.50) = −40 J.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ

items.q: A car of mass 1200 kg starts from rest on a level road. The driving force on it is 4000 N and the total resistive force is 1000 N; both are constant. What is the speed of the car after it has travelled 50 m?
items.why:
The work–energy relation is often introduced with a single force on a smooth surface, so 'work done = gain in kinetic energy' is remembered without the word 'resultant' and is then applied to whichever force the question names. Add the work done by every force (or use the resultant force). A crate pulled at constant velocity has positive work done by the pull and equal negative work done by friction; the net work is zero, so the kinetic energy is unchanged.

Working: F_net = 4000 N − 1000 N = 3000 N. W_net = F_net s = 3000 N × 50 m = 1.5 × 10⁵ J = ΔE_k = ½mv². v = √(2 × 1.5 × 10⁵ J / 1200 kg) = √(250 m² s⁻²) = 15.8 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that work done by the resultant force on a system is equal to the change in the energy of the system

items.q: A student pulls a crate at constant velocity for 5.0 m across a rough, level floor, using a horizontal force of 60 N. Which statement about the work done on the crate is correct?
items.correct: The resultant force does no work, so the crate's kinetic energy does not change.
items.misconception: The pull does 300 J of work on the crate, so the crate's kinetic energy increases by 300 J.
items.why: The work–energy relation is often introduced with a single force on a smooth surface, so 'work done = gain in kinetic energy' is remembered without the word 'resultant' and is then applied to whichever force the question names. Add the work done by every force (or use the resultant force). A crate pulled at constant velocity has positive work done by the pull and equal negative work done by friction; the net work is zero, so the kinetic energy is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: that work done by the resultant force on a system is equal to the change in the energy of the system
items.random_wrong: The pull must be greater than friction, so the resultant force does positive work on it.

items.q: Which quantities are added together to give the mechanical energy of a system?
items.correct: Its kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy.
items.misconception: Its kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, and no other store.
items.why: The first examples of energy conservation, such as a falling ball or a swinging pendulum, involve only kinetic and gravitational potential energy, and many GCSE texts write 'mechanical energy = KE + GPE'. Include elastic potential energy, E_H = ½k(Δx)², whenever a spring, bungee cord, trampoline or other elastic body is part of the system. A bungee jumper's mechanical energy at the lowest point is almost entirely elastic potential energy.
items.specStatementText: that mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy
items.random_wrong: Its kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and internal thermal energy.

items.q: A skier of mass 60 kg starts from rest at the top of a slope and descends through a vertical height of 20 m. At the bottom her speed is 16 m s⁻¹. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the total work done on the skier by friction and air resistance during the descent?
items.why:
Two similar-looking relations are taught in the same topic, W_net = ΔE_k and W_nc = ΔE_mech, and students attach the kinetic energy change to whichever forces are named in the question. Decide which relation fits the forces named. For friction and air resistance, compare the total mechanical energy (E_k + E_p) at the start and the end: W_nc = ΔE_k + ΔE_p. Gravity's contribution is then already included in ΔE_p.

Working: ΔE_k = ½mv² − 0 = ½(60 kg)(16 m s⁻¹)² = 7680 J. ΔE_p = mgΔh = (60 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(−20 m) = −11 760 J. W_nc = ΔE_mech = 7680 J − 11 760 J = −4080 J ≈ −4.1 × 10³ J.
items.specStatementText: that in the absence of frictional, resistive forces, the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved

items.q: Blocks of mass 2.0 kg and 4.0 kg are released from rest at the same height. The 2.0 kg block slides down a steep ramp and the 4.0 kg block down a shallow ramp; the bottoms of the two ramps are at the same level. Both ramps are frictionless and air resistance is negligible. How do their speeds at the bottom compare?
items.correct: They are equal, as each block loses the same potential energy per kilogram.
items.misconception: The 4.0 kg block is faster, because its weight is twice as large.
items.why: This Aristotelian idea is supported by everyday experience with air resistance (a feather and a hammer fall differently in air) and by the fact that a heavier object does have a larger weight. A heavier object has a proportionally larger weight but also a proportionally larger mass to accelerate. In energy terms, each kilogram gains gΔh of kinetic energy per kilogram, whatever the total mass.
items.specStatementText: that in the absence of frictional, resistive forces, the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved
items.random_wrong: The lighter block is faster, because its steeper ramp gives it more acceleration.

items.q: Trolley P has a mass of 2.0 kg and trolley Q has a mass of 8.0 kg. The two trolleys have momenta of the same magnitude. How do their kinetic energies compare?
items.correct: P has four times the kinetic energy of Q.
items.misconception: P and Q have the same kinetic energy.
items.why:
Both quantities depend on mass and speed and are introduced as measures of motion; the vector p = mv and the scalar ½mv² are not clearly distinguished (a confusion documented by Lawson and McDermott, 1987). Use E_k = p²/2m. With p fixed, E_k is inversely proportional to m: a body of one quarter the mass moves four times as fast and has four times the kinetic energy.

Working: E_k = p²/2m, so with equal p: E_k(P)/E_k(Q) = m_Q/m_P = 8.0 kg / 2.0 kg = 4. Check: v_P = 4v_Q, so E_k(P)/E_k(Q) = (2.0 × 16v_Q²)/(8.0 × v_Q²) = 4.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.random_wrong: Q has four times the kinetic energy that P has.
items.working: E_k = p²/2m, so with equal p: E_k(P)/E_k(Q) = m_Q/m_P = 8.0 kg / 2.0 kg = 4. Check: v_P = 4v_Q, so E_k(P)/E_k(Q) = (2.0 × 16v_Q²)/(8.0 × v_Q²) = 4.

items.q: A student of mass 55 kg climbs a staircase from a platform 4.0 m above the ground to a landing 10.0 m above the ground. The staircase is 12 m long, measured along its slope. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the increase in her gravitational potential energy?
items.why:
Textbook problems usually start objects on the ground, where the final height and the change in height are the same, so the distinction never matters until the start is above the ground. Subtract the starting height from the final height. Only differences in gravitational potential energy have physical meaning; the zero level is arbitrary and cancels.

Working: Δh = 10.0 m − 4.0 m = 6.0 m. ΔE_p = mgΔh = (55 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²)(6.0 m) = 3234 J ≈ 3.2 × 10³ J.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²

items.q: A spring of spring constant 180 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 0.10 m and then released to launch a trolley of mass 0.50 kg along a smooth horizontal track. All the elastic potential energy is transferred to the trolley's kinetic energy. What is the speed of the trolley?
items.correct: 1.9 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 6.0 m s⁻¹
items.why:
Hooke's law, F = kΔx, is linear and learned first, so the energy is assumed to follow the same linear pattern. The force grows with Δx AND the distance over which it acts grows with Δx, so the energy grows with (Δx)². Compressing a spring twice as far stores four times the energy.

Working: E_H = ½k(Δx)² = ½(180 N m⁻¹)(0.10 m)² = 0.90 J. ½mv² = 0.90 J, so v = √(2 × 0.90 J / 0.50 kg) = √(3.6 m² s⁻²) = 1.9 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.random_wrong: 2.7 m s⁻¹

items.q: Crane X lifts a load through a height of 10 m in 20 s. Crane Y lifts an identical load through the same height in 40 s. Both lift at constant speed. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Both do equal work, and X develops twice as much power as Y.
items.misconception: X does twice as much work as Y, because it transfers energy faster.
items.why: Everyday usage ('power bill', 'power cut', 'energy drink', 'a powerful engine has more energy') blurs the two, and the units kW and kWh look alike. Always ask 'how much?' (energy, J) or 'how fast?' (power, W). The same energy transferred in half the time needs twice the power; the energy stored in a fuel says nothing about how quickly it burns.
items.specStatementText: that power developed P is the rate of work done, or the rate of energy transfer, as given by P = ΔW/Δt = Fv
items.random_wrong: Y does more work than X, because it applies its force for twice as long.

items.q: An electric hoist raises a load of weight 1600 N vertically at a constant speed of 0.45 m s⁻¹. What is the power developed by the hoist's upward force on the load?
items.why:
Students remember that power involves force and speed but not how they combine, and 'dividing' feels natural because power is 'per second'. Derive it: P = ΔW/Δt = FΔs/Δt = Fv. Check with units: N × m s⁻¹ = J s⁻¹ = W, whereas N ÷ m s⁻¹ = kg s⁻¹, which is not a power.

Working: At constant speed, F = weight = 1600 N. P = Fv = (1600 N)(0.45 m s⁻¹) = 720 W = 7.2 × 10² W.
items.specStatementText: that power developed P is the rate of work done, or the rate of energy transfer, as given by P = ΔW/Δt = Fv
items.working: At constant speed, F = weight = 1600 N. P = Fv = (1600 N)(0.45 m s⁻¹) = 720 W = 7.2 × 10² W.

items.q: A Sankey diagram for a car engine has an input arrow representing 200 kJ of chemical energy from the fuel. It divides into four output arrows: 60 kJ of useful mechanical work, 100 kJ of thermal energy carried away by the exhaust gases, 30 kJ of thermal energy removed by the cooling system, and 10 kJ of sound. What is the efficiency of the engine?
items.why:
Efficiency is discussed as 'how much is useful and how much is wasted', so students divide the two quantities that are named rather than the useful output by the input. Divide by the total input. A ratio of useful to wasted can exceed 1 and is not an efficiency; η must lie between 0 and 1.

Working: η = useful work out / total work in = 60 kJ / 200 kJ = 0.30 = 30%. (Check: 60 + 100 + 30 + 10 = 200 kJ, so the outputs equal the input.)
items.specStatementText: efficiency η in terms of energy transfer or power as given by η = useful work out / total work in = useful power out / total power in
items.working: η = useful work out / total work in = 60 kJ / 200 kJ = 0.30 = 30%. (Check: 60 + 100 + 30 + 10 = 200 kJ, so the outputs equal the input.)

items.q: An electric motor with an efficiency of 0.60 takes an input power of 1.5 kW. It lifts a load of mass 90 kg vertically at constant speed. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the speed of the load?
items.why:
Students misread the conservation principle as 'no energy is wasted', merging 'total energy is conserved' with 'all energy is useful'. Conservation says that useful output + wasted output = input. For a real machine the wasted part is not zero, so useful output = η × input, which is less than the input.

Working: Useful power out = ηP_in = 0.60 × 1500 W = 900 W. F = mg = (90 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²) = 882 N. v = P/F = 900 W / 882 N = 1.02 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: efficiency η in terms of energy transfer or power as given by η = useful work out / total work in = useful power out / total power in
items.working: Useful power out = ηP_in = 0.60 × 1500 W = 900 W. F = mg = (90 kg)(9.8 m s⁻²) = 882 N. v = P/F = 900 W / 882 N = 1.02 m s⁻¹.

items.q: A coal-fired power station has an electrical power output of 600 MW and an overall efficiency of 0.40. The energy density of the coal it burns is 30 MJ kg⁻¹, that is, each kilogram burned releases 30 MJ. What mass of coal must the station burn each second?
items.correct: 50.0 kg s⁻¹
items.misconception: 8.00 kg s⁻¹
items.why:
Students memorize η = out/in as a formula to rearrange without checking whether the answer should be larger or smaller than the given quantity. Sanity-check: the useful output must be smaller than the input. If rearranging gives a useful output larger than the input, the efficiency has been applied the wrong way round.

Working: Input power = output / η = 600 MW / 0.40 = 1500 MW = 1.5 × 10⁹ J s⁻¹. Mass rate = (1.5 × 10⁹ J s⁻¹) / (30 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) = 50.0 kg s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: energy density of the fuel sources.
items.random_wrong: 20.0 kg s⁻¹
items.working: Input power = output / η = 600 MW / 0.40 = 1500 MW = 1.5 × 10⁹ J s⁻¹. Mass rate = (1.5 × 10⁹ J s⁻¹) / (30 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) = 50.0 kg s⁻¹.

items.q: Hydrogen gas at atmospheric pressure releases 120 MJ of energy per kilogram and 0.011 MJ per litre when burned. Petrol releases 46 MJ per kilogram and 34 MJ per litre. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: A litre of petrol releases about 3000 times as much energy as a litre of hydrogen.
items.misconception: A litre of hydrogen releases about 2.6 times the energy of a litre of petrol.
items.why:
Energy density is quoted per kilogram in some sources and per unit volume in others, often under the same name, so students assume the rankings must agree. Check the unit. To convert, multiply the energy per kilogram by the density in kg per unit volume. Hydrogen releases about 120 MJ kg⁻¹ but, as a gas at atmospheric pressure, only about 0.011 MJ per litre.

Working: Per litre: 34 MJ / 0.011 MJ = 3.1 × 10³ ≈ 3000. Per kilogram: 120 MJ / 46 MJ = 2.6 (hydrogen higher).
items.specStatementText: energy density of the fuel sources.
items.random_wrong: A kilogram of petrol releases more energy than a kilogram of hydrogen, as petrol is denser.
items.working: Per litre: 34 MJ / 0.011 MJ = 3.1 × 10³ ≈ 3000. Per kilogram: 120 MJ / 46 MJ = 2.6 (hydrogen higher).

items.q: A block of mass 0.40 kg hangs from a vertical spring of spring constant 50 N m⁻¹. At one instant the block is moving at 1.5 m s⁻¹, its centre is 0.30 m above the level chosen as the zero of gravitational potential energy, and the spring is stretched by 0.20 m from its natural length. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the mechanical energy of the block–spring–Earth system at this instant?
items.why:
The ½ is easy to forget when E = mc² and p = mv are also in memory, and students do not see where it comes from, so it feels arbitrary. Derive it once: a constant resultant force F accelerating a mass from rest gives v² = 2as, so Fs = mas = ½mv². Dropping the ½ doubles E_k, or makes a calculated speed too small by a factor of √2.

Working: Mechanical energy = E_k + E_p + E_H.
E_k = ½mv² = ½ × 0.40 kg × (1.5 m s⁻¹)² = 0.45 J.
E_p = mgh = 0.40 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.30 m = 1.176 J.
E_H = ½k(Δx)² = ½ × 50 N m⁻¹ × (0.20 m)² = 1.0 J.
Total = 0.45 + 1.176 + 1.0 = 2.626 J ≈ 2.6 J (2 s.f.).
items.specStatementText: that mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy
items.working:
Mechanical energy = E_k + E_p + E_H.
E_k = ½mv² = ½ × 0.40 kg × (1.5 m s⁻¹)² = 0.45 J.
E_p = mgh = 0.40 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.30 m = 1.176 J.
E_H = ½k(Δx)² = ½ × 50 N m⁻¹ × (0.20 m)² = 1.0 J.
Total = 0.45 + 1.176 + 1.0 = 2.626 J ≈ 2.6 J (2 s.f.).

items.q: Is energy the same thing as force, and can energy be changed into a force?
items.correct: No. Force (in N) is an interaction that can transfer energy by doing work; energy (in J) is a conserved quantity. Energy is never converted into a force.
items.misconception: Energy and force are the same kind of thing, so energy can be turned into a force such as friction or the push of the floor.
items.why: In everyday speech 'force', 'energy' and 'power' are used interchangeably ('a forceful, energetic, powerful player'), and students meet force and energy in the same mechanics lessons. A force transfers energy only when its point of application moves, and the amount transferred is the work done, W = Fs cos θ. The force itself is not a store of energy and cannot be where 'missing' energy has gone; that energy is in some other store, such as internal energy.
items.specStatementText: the principle of the conservation of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the conservation of energy mean that each object keeps the same amount of energy?
items.correct: No. Conservation applies to the total energy of an isolated system. Energy can move between objects, so any single object may gain or lose energy.
items.misconception: Conservation of energy means every object in a system keeps the same amount of energy throughout a process.
items.why: Students apply the principle without first choosing a system, so 'energy is conserved' is read as a statement about whichever object is being discussed, such as the ball or the car. Always define the system first. Within an isolated system, energy transferred out of one object is transferred into others, and only the total is constant. A ball that slows down has less kinetic energy; the total is conserved because the air, floor and ball's internal energy gained exactly what it lost.
items.specStatementText: the principle of the conservation of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is work a form of energy that a body possesses?
items.correct: No. Work is a process of transferring energy by a force. A body has energy in stores such as kinetic or potential energy; it does not have or contain 'work'.
items.misconception: Work is a kind of energy that is stored in a body, so the work done on a body can be listed alongside its kinetic and potential energy.
items.why: Work and energy share the unit joule and the equation 'work done = energy transferred' is memorized, so students treat work as another energy store rather than as a transfer. Work done measures energy transferred by a force. After the transfer, the energy is in a store (kinetic, gravitational or elastic potential, internal). Adding the work done to the stores double-counts the same energy.
items.specStatementText: that work done by a force is equivalent to a transfer of energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a working device always transfer most of its input energy usefully?
items.correct: No. Many common devices transfer only a small fraction usefully; a filament lamp emits less than a tenth of its input as light, and a petrol car engine transfers roughly 20–35% usefully.
items.misconception: A device is built for its purpose, so its useful output must be the largest output, and the useful arrow on a Sankey diagram must be the widest.
items.why: Devices are described by their purpose (a lamp 'makes light', a motor 'lifts loads'), so students assume the purpose dominates the energy flow and are surprised by real efficiencies. The widths of the arrows are set by measured energies, not by purpose. In a filament lamp the arrow for energy transferred to the surroundings by heating is many times wider than the light arrow.
items.specStatementText: that energy transfers can be represented on a Sankey diagram
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which trigonometric function gives the component of a force along the displacement?
items.correct: The cosine of the angle between the force and the displacement: the component along the displacement is F cos θ.
items.misconception: The component of the force along the displacement is F sin θ, or sine and cosine are interchangeable.
items.why: Students resolve forces in many contexts where the angle is measured from different lines (for example from the vertical on a slope), and they memorize 'sin for one component, cos for the other' without tying it to which angle is given. Identify the angle θ between the force and the displacement. The component adjacent to that angle, along the displacement, is F cos θ, so W = Fs cos θ. Use sin only if the angle given is measured from the perpendicular direction.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can cos θ be evaluated with the calculator in radian mode when θ is given in degrees?
items.correct: No. An angle given in degrees must be evaluated with the calculator in degree mode (or converted to radians first).
items.misconception: The calculator mode does not matter, so cos 30 gives the cosine of 30° whatever the setting.
items.why: Calculators are often left in radian mode after work on circular motion or oscillations, and the result (for example cos 30 rad ≈ 0.154) is not obviously wrong unless checked. Check the mode before evaluating a trigonometric function, and sanity-check: cos 30° ≈ 0.87, so W for a force at 30° should be a little less than Fs.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is there a real outward (centrifugal) force on a body in uniform circular motion?
items.correct: No. In an inertial frame the only horizontal force on the body is the inward (centripetal) force; there is no outward force. The body's velocity is tangential at every instant, perpendicular to that inward force.
items.misconception: A body moving in a circle has a real outward centrifugal force acting on it, which balances the inward pull.
items.why: From inside a turning car or on a roundabout, people feel pushed outward, and the word 'centrifugal' is used in everyday language as if it named a real outward force. The outward push felt in a turning car is the body's tendency to continue in a straight line, described from the turning frame. In an inertial frame there is no outward force: the inward force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so it changes the direction of the velocity, not the speed, and does no work.
items.specStatementText: that work W done on a body by a constant force depends on the component of the force along the line of displacement as given by W = Fs cos θ
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the resultant of two opposing forces found by adding their magnitudes?
items.correct: No. Forces are vectors: two opposing forces along a line give a resultant equal to the difference of their magnitudes, in the direction of the larger.
items.misconception: The resultant force is the sum of the sizes of all the forces acting, whatever their directions.
items.why: Students first meet 'total' as arithmetic addition and carry it over to forces, treating them as scalars. Difficulties with vector addition are well documented among introductory physics students (e.g. Nguyen and Meltzer, 2003). Choose a positive direction and add the forces with signs: 4000 N forward and 1000 N backward give a resultant of 3000 N forward. Only the resultant force determines the change in kinetic energy.
items.specStatementText: that work done by the resultant force on a system is equal to the change in the energy of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is internal (thermal) energy part of the mechanical energy of a system?
items.correct: No. Mechanical energy is kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy of the bodies as a whole. Internal energy, the random kinetic and potential energy of the particles, is separate.
items.misconception: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy of particles, so it counts as part of a system's mechanical energy.
items.why: Students learn that temperature relates to particle kinetic energy and reason that all kinetic energy is mechanical energy. Mechanical energy refers to the ordered motion and position of whole bodies. When friction acts, mechanical energy decreases and internal energy increases by the same amount; that transfer only makes sense if internal energy is not counted as mechanical.
items.specStatementText: that mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and elastic potential energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On a frictionless slope, does the speed at the bottom depend on how steep the slope is?
items.correct: No. With no friction, the speed at the bottom depends only on the vertical drop: ½mv² = mgΔh gives v = √(2gΔh) for any shape of slope.
items.misconception: A steeper slope gives a greater speed at the bottom, because the object accelerates more.
items.why: A steeper slope does give a larger acceleration, which students observe correctly; they then assume larger acceleration must mean larger final speed, without noting the shorter distance. On a steeper slope the acceleration is larger but the distance is shorter; on a shallow slope the acceleration is smaller but the distance is longer. The energy argument shows the two effects cancel exactly: equal drops in height give equal speeds.
items.specStatementText: that in the absence of frictional, resistive forces, the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an object that accelerates for longer on a frictionless slope reach a greater speed?
items.correct: Not necessarily. On a shallow slope it accelerates for longer but at a smaller rate; the final speed depends only on the height dropped.
items.misconception: An object that spends more time accelerating, as on a long shallow slope, must end up with a greater speed.
items.why: From kinematics (v = u + at) students learn that speed grows with time, and apply it without noting that the acceleration a is smaller on the shallow slope. The speed gained is v = at, with both a and t depending on the slope. The energy method bypasses this: ½mv² = mgΔh, so equal drops give equal speeds whatever the slope.
items.specStatementText: that in the absence of frictional, resistive forces, the total mechanical energy of a system is conserved
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is kinetic energy proportional to speed?
items.correct: No. E_k = ½mv², so kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed, so doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy (the square is dropped).
items.why: Many relationships met early are linear, and momentum p = mv is proportional to speed, so students expect kinetic energy to behave the same way. Always square the speed. Halving the speed leaves one quarter of the kinetic energy; this is why braking distances grow much faster than speed.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the heavier of two bodies always have more kinetic energy?
items.correct: No. Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, E_k = ½mv²; a lighter body moving fast enough has more kinetic energy.
items.misconception: The heavier body has more kinetic energy, because kinetic energy depends mainly on mass.
items.why: Heavy moving objects are the ones that do damage in everyday experience, so students associate energy with mass and overlook the speed dependence. Compare using the full expression. For equal momenta, E_k = p²/2m, so the heavier body has LESS kinetic energy; its speed is lower in proportion to its greater mass, and speed enters squared.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When comparing kinetic energies of two bodies, can the speed ratio be used on its own?
items.correct: No. E_k depends on both m and v². The ratio of kinetic energies is (m₁/m₂)(v₁/v₂)², so the mass ratio must be included.
items.misconception: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed, so the ratio of kinetic energies is just the square of the speed ratio, whatever the masses.
items.why: Students correctly remember that 'speed is squared' and focus on the variable that changes most, a form of single-variable reasoning common in proportional-reasoning tasks. Write the ratio in full, E_k1/E_k2 = (m₁v₁²)/(m₂v₂²). For two bodies with equal momentum and a 1 : 4 mass ratio, the speed ratio is 4 : 1, so (1/4) × 16 = 4, not 16.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the change in gravitational potential energy depend on the path length travelled?
items.correct: No. It depends only on the vertical change in height, ΔE_p = mgΔh; the length and shape of the path do not matter.
items.misconception: The gain in gravitational potential energy is the weight multiplied by the distance travelled along the path, such as the length of a slope or staircase.
items.why: Work is met as 'force × distance', and students use the distance given in the question without asking whether it lies along the weight. The weight acts vertically, so only the vertical displacement counts: along a slope of length s at angle θ to the horizontal, the work against gravity is mg × s sin θ = mgΔh.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is mass in kilograms the same as weight in newtons?
items.correct: No. Mass (kg) is the amount of matter; weight (N) is the gravitational force on it, W = mg. Near the Earth's surface a 1 kg mass has a weight of about 9.8 N.
items.misconception: Mass and weight are the same quantity, so the mass in kilograms can be used where a force in newtons is needed, or a weight in newtons can be multiplied by g again.
items.why: In everyday language 'weight' is measured in kilograms, and bathroom scales read in kg, so the two quantities are merged. Check units: ΔE_p = mgΔh needs mass in kg multiplied by g; a force already given in newtons is a weight and must not be multiplied by g again.
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²

items.q: Is the energy stored in a stretched spring equal to the final force multiplied by the extension?
items.correct: No. The force rises from zero to kΔx during stretching, so the work done is the average force times the extension: E_H = ½k(Δx)², half of kΔx × Δx.
items.misconception: The work done stretching a spring is the final force multiplied by the extension, W = kΔx × Δx.
items.why: Students apply W = Fs with a single value of force, as they do for constant forces, not recognizing that the spring force varies during the stretch. The work done is the area under the force–extension graph, which is a triangle for a Hooke's-law spring: ½ × kΔx × Δx = ½k(Δx)².
items.specStatementText: that if mechanical energy is conserved, work is the amount of energy transformed between different forms of mechanical energy in a system, such as: ◦ the kinetic energy of translational motion as given by E_k = ½mv² = p²/2m ◦ the gravitational potential energy, when close to the surface of the Earth as given by ΔE_p = mgΔh ◦ the elastic potential energy as given by E_H = ½k(Δx)²

items.q: Is power the same as force or strength?
items.correct: No. Power is the rate of doing work, P = Fv; a large force on something that moves slowly may involve little power.
items.misconception: A more powerful machine is one that exerts a larger force, so power can be found from the force alone.
items.why: In everyday language 'powerful' means strong, and 'power' is used for force in sport and advertising. Power depends on force AND speed: P = Fv. Two cranes exerting the same force on identical loads develop different powers if they lift them at different speeds.
items.specStatementText: that power developed P is the rate of work done, or the rate of energy transfer, as given by P = ΔW/Δt = Fv
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does efficiency measure the fraction of energy that is wasted?
items.correct: No. Efficiency is the fraction transferred usefully. The fraction wasted is 1 − η.
items.misconception: Efficiency is a measure of the energy lost, so the fraction wasted is the efficiency (and the useful fraction is 1 − η).
items.why: Discussions of efficiency focus on reducing waste, so the number becomes attached to the waste rather than to the useful output. η = useful out / total in. A power station with η = 0.40 transfers 40% of the input usefully and dissipates 60%.
items.specStatementText: efficiency η in terms of energy transfer or power as given by η = useful work out / total work in = useful power out / total power in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a denser or heavier fuel release more energy per kilogram?
items.correct: No. Energy released per kilogram depends on the chemical (or nuclear) reactions of the fuel, not on its density; hydrogen, the least dense fuel, releases the most energy per kilogram of any chemical fuel.
items.misconception: A denser, heavier-feeling fuel contains more energy in each kilogram.
items.why: Students associate 'heavy' and 'dense' with 'containing more', which is true per unit volume but is then carried over to 'per kilogram', where density cancels. Energy per kilogram is fixed by the energy released in the reaction per unit mass of fuel. Density only affects how much of that mass fits into a given volume.
items.specStatementText: energy density of the fuel sources.
